A graph has no shape of its own: its nodes and edges say what is linked to what, but not where
anything should go on a page. A *layout* assigns each node a position, and the choice of layout
largely decides what a drawing shows. A force-directed layout reveals clusters, a layered layout
reveals a hierarchy, a circle makes every edge visible, and a map shows where things really are.

[Static plots](22-plotting.qmd) introduced the three layouts built into `plot()`: `"force"`,
`"circular"`, and `"random"`. This page covers the `layout_*()` methods, which offer many more
algorithms and finer control, and shows how to draw nodes at coordinates that come with the data.

## How layout methods work

Every `layout_*()` method computes a position for each node and stores it as an `[x, y]` list in a
node attribute, `"pos"` by default. Passing the name of that attribute to `plot()` as `layout=`
draws the graph at those positions. The
[Kamada–Kawai layout](../reference/Graph.layout_kamada_kawai.qmd) of the karate club:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec
import polars as pl

karate = ec.karate_club()
karate.layout_kamada_kawai()
karate.get_node_df().select("id", "label", "pos").head(3)
```

The positions are centered on the origin and scaled so that the largest coordinate is 1; `scale=`
and `center=` change both. `plot()` then fits them to the canvas, keeping their proportions, with
the `y` axis pointing up:

```{python}
karate.plot(layout="pos", label_by="label", node_size=10, height=500)
```

Since the positions are stored on the graph, the same layout can be drawn again and again, with
different colors or labels, without being recomputed, and the drawings stay comparable. Positions
given with `layout="pos"` are taken as they are, so `plot()` doesn't push overlapping nodes apart;
a smaller `node_size=` is often needed to keep the nodes from touching.

Two arguments are shared by all of the methods. `attr_name=` stores the positions under another
name, so that several layouts can be kept side by side on one graph, and `return_dict=True`
returns the positions as a dictionary from node ID to `(x, y)` instead of storing them, which is
useful when the coordinates are needed for something other than drawing:

```{python}
positions = karate.layout_circular(return_dict=True)
len(positions), [round(value, 3) for value in positions[2]]
```

The dictionary has an entry for each of the 34 members, and node 2 sits just counterclockwise of
node 1, which the circular layout puts at the rightmost point of the circle.

## Force-directed layouts

Force-directed layouts treat the graph as a physical system. Linked nodes attract each other like
the ends of a spring, all nodes repel each other like charged particles, and the layout is the
state in which the forces balance. Closely knit groups pull together and loosely linked parts drift
apart, which is why these layouts are the default choice for most networks. EdgeCase has four,
which differ in the forces they use and so in the pictures they draw. The dolphin network, with its
two loosely linked communities, shows the differences well.

[`layout_spring()`](../reference/Graph.layout_spring.qmd) is the classic Fruchterman–Reingold
algorithm, the same one behind `plot(layout="force")`. It spreads the nodes fairly evenly over the
available space:

```{python}
dolphins = ec.dolphins()
dolphins.layout_spring(seed=1, attr_name="spring")
dolphins.plot(layout="spring", show_labels=False, node_size=6)
```

The two communities are visible on the left and the right, linked by a few animals. Like all layouts
that start from random positions, it takes a `seed=` for a reproducible result. `k=` sets the ideal
distance between linked nodes, and `iterations=` the number of steps, 50 by default, which is
usually enough for a few hundred nodes.

[`layout_kamada_kawai()`](../reference/Graph.layout_kamada_kawai.qmd) works differently. It tries
to make the distance between every pair of nodes on the page proportional to their shortest-path
distance in the graph, so that two nodes three steps apart are drawn three times as far apart as
two neighbors:

```{python}
dolphins.layout_kamada_kawai(attr_name="kk")
dolphins.plot(layout="kk", show_labels=False, node_size=6)
```

The result is more compact, with more uniform edge lengths. Distances on the page can be read as
distances in the graph, which makes this layout a good choice for paths, trees, and grids, whose
global shape it draws faithfully. It starts from a circle rather than from random positions, so it
needs no seed and always gives the same drawing.

[`layout_forceatlas2()`](../reference/Graph.layout_forceatlas2.qmd) is the ForceAtlas2 algorithm of
the Gephi software, widely used for social networks. Its options correspond to the ones in Gephi.
The most useful, `linlog=True`, weakens the attraction between distant nodes, which separates
clusters much more sharply:

```{python}
dolphins.layout_forceatlas2(linlog=True, seed=1, attr_name="linlog")
dolphins.plot(layout="linlog", show_labels=False, node_size=6)
```

The two communities are now clearly apart, joined by a narrow bridge of the few animals that move
between them. This makes LinLog mode a natural companion to community detection. The other options
of ForceAtlas2 are `gravity=`, which pulls everything toward the center and keeps disconnected
pieces from drifting away, `dissuade_hubs=True`, which pushes hubs to the edges of their clusters,
and `node_size=`, which keeps nodes of given sizes from overlapping.

[`layout_arf()`](../reference/Graph.layout_arf.qmd), the *attractive and repulsive forces* layout,
links every pair of nodes with a weak spring, and linked pairs with a stronger one:

```{python}
dolphins.layout_arf(seed=1, attr_name="arf")
dolphins.plot(layout="arf", show_labels=False, node_size=6)
```

The weak springs hold the whole layout in an evenly filled disc without large gaps, at the cost of
much of the visible community structure. It suits graphs without strong clusters, where the other
layouts tend to leave holes.

Every force-directed method costs time proportional to the square of the number of nodes at each
step, so they are practical up to a few thousand nodes. `layout_spring()`, `layout_kamada_kawai()`,
and `layout_forceatlas2()` take `weighted=` to use the edge weights: heavier edges pull harder in
the spring and ForceAtlas2 layouts, while Kamada–Kawai treats weights as lengths, so heavier edges
are drawn longer.

## Layered layouts

Hierarchies, pipelines, and two-mode networks are clearer when their nodes are drawn in layers.

[`layout_bfs()`](../reference/Graph.layout_bfs.qmd) puts a start node in the first layer, its
neighbors in the second, their neighbors in the third, and so on, so that each node's layer is its
distance from the start. The small organization of [Static plots](22-plotting.qmd):

```{python}
org = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_edges(
    [
        ("Dana", "Eli"),
        ("Dana", "Fay"),
        ("Eli", "Gus"),
        ("Eli", "Hal"),
        ("Fay", "Ivy"),
        ("Gus", "Hal"),
        ("Fay", "Eli"),
    ],
    auto_create_nodes=True,
)
org.layout_bfs(start="Dana")
org.plot(layout="pos", label_by="label", node_size=12, width=500, height=300)
```

Dana, at the top of the organization, is on the left, followed by the two managers that report to
Dana and then the three people below them. The layers run from left to right; `align="horizontal"`
stacks them from bottom to top instead. On a directed graph the search follows the edge
directions, and every node must be reachable from the start node.

[`layout_multipartite()`](../reference/Graph.layout_multipartite.qmd) takes the layers from a node
attribute instead, which suits any graph whose nodes have a stage, a level, or a rank. A small
neural network, with its three layers of units:

```{python}
layers = {"input": ["x1", "x2", "x3"], "hidden": ["h1", "h2", "h3", "h4"], "output": ["y1", "y2"]}
net = ec.Graph(directed=True)
for level, units in enumerate(layers.values()):
    for unit in units:
        net.add_node(unit, layer=level)

inputs, hidden, outputs = layers.values()
net.add_edges([(a, b) for a in inputs for b in hidden] + [(a, b) for a in hidden for b in outputs])
net.layout_multipartite(subset_key="layer")
net.plot(layout="pos", label_by="label", node_size=12, width=500, height=300)
```

The layers are drawn in sorted order of the attribute's values, and `subset_key=` can also be a
dictionary from layer value to a list of nodes, when the layers aren't stored on the graph.

[`layout_bipartite()`](../reference/Graph.layout_bipartite.qmd) is the two-layer case, for
affiliation networks of people and the groups or events they belong to. Its `nodes=` argument
names the nodes of one side. In the Southern Women network, the `bipartite` attribute marks the
women with 0 and the events with 1:

```{python}
davis = ec.davis_southern_women()
women = davis.get_node_df().filter(pl.col("bipartite") == 0)["id"].to_list()
davis.layout_bipartite(nodes=women)
davis.plot(layout="pos", label_by="label", node_size=6, width=600, height=520)
```

The women are on the left and the fourteen social events on the right. Without `nodes=`, the
method splits the graph into two sides itself, and raises an error if the graph is not bipartite.

## Circles and shells

[`layout_circular()`](../reference/Graph.layout_circular.qmd) places the nodes evenly around a
circle in the order of their IDs. Since the edges play no part, the picture shows how the order
relates to the structure. In the karate club, whose members are numbered in no meaningful order,
the edges cross the circle in every direction:

```{python}
karate.layout_circular()
karate.plot(layout="pos", color_by="faction", show_labels=False, node_size=8, width=400, height=400)
```

The nodes are colored by faction with `color_by=` (see [Aesthetics](24-aesthetics.qmd)), and the
two factions are mixed all around the circle. A better order puts linked nodes next to each other.
[`layout_shell()`](../reference/Graph.layout_shell.qmd) places the nodes on one or more circles,
and takes the nodes of each circle in the order given, so a single circle in the
[spectral order](21-spectral.qmd#ordering-nodes-with-the-fiedler-vector) of the club makes a much
more readable drawing:

```{python}
karate.layout_shell(nlist=[karate.spectral_ordering()])
karate.plot(layout="pos", color_by="faction", show_labels=False, node_size=8, width=400, height=400)
```

Each faction now occupies one half of the circle, most edges run between nearby nodes along the
rim, and the few edges that cross the middle are the friendships between the factions.

With several shells, `nlist=` lists them from the innermost outward, and a first shell with a
single node puts that node at the center. This shows a node's neighborhood at a glance. For the
Medici, with their marriage partners in the first ring and the other families in the second:

```{python}
florentine = ec.florentine_families()
medici = florentine.get_node_df().filter(pl.col("label") == "Medici")["id"].item()
partners = florentine.neighbors(medici)
others = [node for node in florentine.get_node_df()["id"] if node != medici and node not in partners]

florentine.layout_shell(nlist=[[medici], partners, others])
florentine.plot(layout="pos", label_by="label", node_size=10, width=500, height=450)
```

Six of the fifteen families are married into the Medici directly, and most of the rest are only a
step further out. `nlist=` can also name a node attribute, in which case nodes that share a value
form a shell, in sorted order of the values. [`layout_spiral()`](../reference/Graph.layout_spiral.qmd)
places the nodes along a spiral in ID order, which packs long sequences, such as a chain of events
in time, more compactly than a circle.

## Layouts from structure

Two layouts derive the positions from a mathematical property of the graph.

[`layout_spectral()`](../reference/Graph.layout_spectral.qmd) uses two eigenvectors of the
Laplacian matrix as coordinates. It recovers the geometry of meshes and grids from their edges
alone, but tends to squeeze social networks into a small area; [Matrices and spectra](21-spectral.qmd#spectral-layouts)
has an example. [`layout_planar()`](../reference/Graph.layout_planar.qmd) draws a planar graph so
that no two edges cross, which proves that the graph is planar, but the nodes are placed on a grid
in a broad triangle and the drawing can be cramped. A force-directed layout often draws a planar
graph without crossings as well, and looks better. Planarity itself is covered in
[Coloring, matching, and covering](20-coloring-matching.qmd).

[`layout_random()`](../reference/Graph.layout_random.qmd) scatters the nodes uniformly at random.
It shows nothing of the structure, which makes it a useful baseline: a random drawing shows how
much of the apparent structure in another layout is real.

## Coordinates from the data

Many networks come with positions of their own: stations and cities have coordinates, components
of a circuit have places on a board, and cells of a tissue have places under a microscope. Such
positions can be stored in a node attribute directly and drawn with `layout=`. A network of fast
rail links between European cities, with each city at its longitude and latitude:

```{python}
cities = {
    "London": (-0.13, 51.51), "Paris": (2.35, 48.86), "Brussels": (4.35, 50.85),
    "Amsterdam": (4.90, 52.37), "Cologne": (6.96, 50.94), "Frankfurt": (8.68, 50.11),
    "Lyon": (4.84, 45.76), "Zurich": (8.54, 47.37), "Milan": (9.19, 45.46),
    "Munich": (11.58, 48.14), "Berlin": (13.40, 52.52),
}
links = [
    ("London", "Paris"), ("London", "Brussels"), ("Paris", "Brussels"),
    ("Brussels", "Amsterdam"), ("Brussels", "Cologne"), ("Amsterdam", "Cologne"),
    ("Cologne", "Frankfurt"), ("Frankfurt", "Munich"), ("Frankfurt", "Berlin"),
    ("Paris", "Lyon"), ("Paris", "Frankfurt"), ("Paris", "Zurich"), ("Zurich", "Milan"),
    ("Lyon", "Milan"), ("Munich", "Berlin"), ("Zurich", "Munich"),
]
rail = ec.Graph().add_nodes(list(cities)).add_edges(links)
rail.set_node_attrs("lonlat", {city: list(point) for city, point in cities.items()})
rail.plot(layout="lonlat", label_by="label", node_size=6, width=500, height=450)
```

The dictionary passed to `set_node_attrs()` is keyed by labels, which EdgeCase resolves to node IDs.
The map is recognizable, but stretched from east to west: a degree of longitude is shorter than a
degree of latitude away from the equator, by a factor of the cosine of the latitude. Scaling the
longitudes by the cosine of the map's central latitude, about 49°, gives a simple projection that
is accurate enough for a map of this size:

```{python}
import math

shrink = math.cos(math.radians(49))
rail.set_node_attrs("map", {city: [lon * shrink, lat] for city, (lon, lat) in cities.items()})
rail.plot(layout="map", label_by="label", node_size=6, width=500, height=450)
```

`plot()` fits any coordinates to the canvas, so they can be in degrees, meters, or pixels. To bring
positions from elsewhere into the same frame as the `layout_*()` methods, centered on the origin
with a largest coordinate of 1, [`rescale_layout()`](../reference/Graph.rescale_layout.qmd)
centers and resizes them without changing their shape.

### Filling in missing positions

When only some of the nodes have known positions, a force-directed layout can place the rest.
`initial=` gives the starting positions, either as a node attribute or a dictionary, and `fixed=`
lists the nodes that must stay where they are. Adding Lille and Strasbourg to the rail network
without coordinates, and letting `layout_spring()` place them among their neighbors:

```{python}
rail.add_nodes(["Lille", "Strasbourg"]).add_edges(
    [
        ("Lille", "London"), ("Lille", "Paris"), ("Lille", "Brussels"),
        ("Strasbourg", "Paris"), ("Strasbourg", "Frankfurt"), ("Strasbourg", "Zurich"),
    ]
)
rail.layout_spring(initial="map", fixed=list(cities), k=0.5, iterations=200, seed=1, attr_name="map")
rail.plot(layout="map", label_by="label", node_size=6, width=500, height=450)
```

The two new cities settle between the cities they are linked to: Lille between London, Paris, and
Brussels, and Strasbourg between Paris, Frankfurt, and Zurich, not far from where they really
are. The ideal edge length `k=` needs attention here. By default it is set for a layout in a unit
square, and with coordinates in degrees, the repulsion from all the fixed cities would push the new
nodes far outside the map; a small `k=` lets the pull of their links dominate. With `fixed=`, the
result is not rescaled, so the fixed nodes keep their exact coordinates.

The same arguments refine a layout step by step. `initial="pos"` continues from an earlier layout
rather than from random positions, which keeps a drawing stable when a few nodes or edges are
added, and `initial=` combined with `fixed=` can pin a few landmark nodes, such as the leaders of
two groups, to opposite sides of the drawing.

## Choosing a layout

| Method | Places nodes by | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| [`layout_spring()`](../reference/Graph.layout_spring.qmd) | springs and repulsion (Fruchterman–Reingold) | general networks |
| [`layout_kamada_kawai()`](../reference/Graph.layout_kamada_kawai.qmd) | page distance matching graph distance | paths, trees, grids, small networks |
| [`layout_forceatlas2()`](../reference/Graph.layout_forceatlas2.qmd) | ForceAtlas2, optionally LinLog | social networks with communities |
| [`layout_arf()`](../reference/Graph.layout_arf.qmd) | springs between all pairs | graphs without strong clusters |
| [`layout_bfs()`](../reference/Graph.layout_bfs.qmd) | distance from a start node | trees and hierarchies |
| [`layout_multipartite()`](../reference/Graph.layout_multipartite.qmd) | a layer attribute | pipelines, staged processes |
| [`layout_bipartite()`](../reference/Graph.layout_bipartite.qmd) | two sides | affiliation and user–item networks |
| [`layout_circular()`](../reference/Graph.layout_circular.qmd) | ID order around a circle | rings, chord diagrams |
| [`layout_shell()`](../reference/Graph.layout_shell.qmd) | concentric circles, in a given order | neighborhoods, groups, custom orders |
| [`layout_spiral()`](../reference/Graph.layout_spiral.qmd) | ID order along a spiral | long sequences |
| [`layout_spectral()`](../reference/Graph.layout_spectral.qmd) | Laplacian eigenvectors | meshes and grids |
| [`layout_planar()`](../reference/Graph.layout_planar.qmd) | a crossing-free embedding | showing planarity |
| [`layout_random()`](../reference/Graph.layout_random.qmd) | chance | a baseline |

For a network that is new to you, a force-directed layout is the place to start. If the drawing is a
tangle, `layout_forceatlas2(linlog=True)` often separates the groups, and if the graph has a known
hierarchy, order, or geography, a layout that uses it will show more than any general-purpose
algorithm can.
